title: Make a crop and cultivar choice for your region

lessons.title: Knowing your region
lessons.html:
Knowing your region

Before you decide what to plant, you must know your area well. A crop that grows well in one place may fail in another. South Africa has many different climates: summer rain on the Highveld and in KwaZulu-Natal, winter rain in the Western Cape, hot and dry areas in the Northern Cape and Limpopo, and frost in the high areas.

Things to find out about your farm

  • Rain: how much falls in a year, and in which months. Summer-rainfall areas suit crops like maize, sorghum, soybeans and dry beans. Winter-rainfall areas suit wheat, barley and canola.
  • Temperature: how hot it gets in summer and how cold in winter. Some crops, like bananas and mangoes, cannot take frost.
  • Frost dates: when the first and last frost usually happen. This sets the planting window.
  • Soil: sandy or clay, deep or shallow, acid or not. Do a soil test.
  • Water for irrigation: is there a borehole, river or dam, and do you have the right to use the water?
  • Slope and drainage: steep land erodes; low land may waterlog.
  • Pests and diseases common in the area.

Where to get information

  • Neighbouring farmers: what grows well for them?
  • The local extension officer from the Department of Agriculture.
  • The Agricultural Research Council (ARC) and grain or commodity organisations, which publish cultivar trial results.
  • Seed company representatives.
  • Your own farm records from past seasons.

Example

Mpho farms near Bethlehem in the eastern Free State. Rain falls mainly from October to March, winters are cold with heavy frost, and her soils are deep sandy loam. Maize, soybeans, sunflower and dry beans are suitable summer crops. Avocados and bananas would not survive her frost.

lessons.title: Choosing the crop and the cultivar
lessons.html:
Choosing the crop and the cultivar

Choosing the crop

Once you know what can grow in your region, ask:

  1. Is there a market? Who will buy it, at what price, and how far is the market? Fresh vegetables need buyers nearby; grain can go to a silo.
  2. What does it cost to grow? Seed, fertiliser, chemicals, labour, fuel and transport.
  3. Do I have the equipment and skills? Can I plant, spray and harvest it?
  4. What is the risk? Hail, drought, pests and price drops.
  5. Does it fit my rotation? Changing crops each season, for example maize after soybeans, helps the soil and reduces pests.

What is a cultivar?

A cultivar is a variety of a crop, bred to have certain qualities. For example, there are many maize cultivars. They differ in:

QualityWhy it matters
Growing season length (early, medium, late)Short-season cultivars suit areas with early frost or late planting
Yield potentialHow much it can produce in good conditions
Drought toleranceImportant in dry areas without irrigation
Disease and pest resistanceFewer sprays and less loss
Grain or fruit qualityMust meet the buyer's standard, such as white or yellow maize

Making the choice

  • Look at local trial results over several seasons, not just one good year.
  • Choose cultivars that do well in conditions like yours.
  • Plant more than one cultivar to spread the risk.
  • Buy certified seed from a registered seller, so it is true to type and grows well.
  • Record how each cultivar performs on your farm.

Example

Mpho chose a medium-season yellow maize cultivar with good drought tolerance, because her local feed mill buys yellow maize and the frost comes early in autumn.

Key points

  • Know your region's rainfall, temperatures, frost, soil and water.
  • Get advice from neighbours, extension officers, the ARC and trial results.
  • Choose a crop with a market, a cost you can afford and a risk you can manage.
  • A cultivar is a variety with its own season length, yield, tolerance and quality.
  • Buy certified seed and spread risk by planting more than one cultivar.
